qs.q: What pooled nasopharyngeal MRSA carriage prevalence did the meta-analysis find, from how many studies and participants, and with what heterogeneity and prediction interval?
qs.a: 7.3% (95% CI 5.0-10.8) from 20 studies and 6869 participants; I2=95.5%; prediction interval 1.30% to 42.0%

qs.q: What pooled odds ratios did the paper report for prior hospitalization and previous antibiotic use, and is the paper consistent with itself?
qs.a: Results table: hospitalization OR 4.48 (95% CI 2.62-7.67), antibiotics OR 2.41 (1.22-4.73). The abstract gives different figures (3.49 and 2.35), so the paper is internally inconsistent; a good answer notes this.

qs.q: What did the trim-and-fill analysis do to the pooled prevalence, and how do the authors treat that corrected figure?
qs.a: Nine studies were imputed and the pooled prevalence rose to 14.77% (95% CI 8.96-24.37) from 7.3%; the authors call it exploratory, based on assumptions, to be interpreted with caution (Egger p<0.001, Begg p=0.0003 showed asymmetry)

qs.q: Does the paper show that HIV patients have significantly higher carriage than school children?
qs.a: Not directly. The subgroup point estimates are 13.8% (95% CI 3.5-54.9) vs 3.1% (0.8-11.6), with overlapping intervals and no pairwise test. The only significant result is in the multivariable meta-regression, where HIV studies were higher than the reference group of college students (beta 0.99, 95% CI 0.19-1.79).

qs.q: Which antibiotics showed the highest and lowest pooled resistance, and which pooled estimate had low heterogeneity?
qs.a: Highest tetracycline 55.75% (45.54-68.25), then trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 49.88% and erythromycin 44.42%; lowest clindamycin 12.66% (8.21-19.53), which also had the lowest heterogeneity (I2=27.2%)

qs.q: What limitations of the evidence do the authors list?
qs.a: Residual heterogeneity, English-only search, studies from only a few regions, publication bias, inconsistent variable definitions across studies that prevented pooling other risk factors, and wide intervals for antibiotics with few studies

qs.q: Did the authors find a trend in MRSA prevalence over 2015 to 2025?
qs.a: No. Meta-regression found no significant temporal trend (p=0.9369); predicted prevalence stayed roughly constant

qs.q: The Discussion says wounds, respiratory infection and skin lesions were significantly associated with MRSA colonization. Do the Results agree?
qs.a: No. In the Results their odds ratios have confidence intervals including 1 (wound 1.95, 0.40-9.51; respiratory infection 3.62, 0.56-23.59; skin lesions 2.76, 0.25-30.68), so they were not significant; only hospitalization and prior antibiotic use were

qs.q: What SCCmec types were found among the MRSA isolates?
qs.a: NOT STATED. Molecular typing (SCCmec, spa, virulence factors) is listed only as future work; all included studies used cefoxitin disc diffusion

qs.q: What was the pooled MRSA carriage prevalence in children under five years old?
qs.a: NOT STATED. Only school children (3.1%) are reported as a subgroup
